newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade protesters welcome OSCE support.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade protesters welcome OSCE support.

text.p: Police on Friday blocked tens of thousands of anti-government protesters trying to march in Belgrade for a 38th straight day as the OSCE backed Serbian opposition claims that it was robbed in recent local elections.

Former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, representing the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe (OSCE), confirmed opposition victories over Slobodan Milosevic and his ruling SPS party in a series of disputed municipalities.

Gonzalez, who headed an OSCE fact-finding mission to Belgrade last week, called on the OSCE to issue an "urgent appeal" to authorities and political forces in Yugoslavia to "comply with the will expressed at the polls by the citizens".

He said authorities should accept opposition victories in Pirot, Kraljevo, Uzice, Smederevska Palanka, Vrasac, Soko Banja, Kraguejevac, Pancevo, Jagodina, Nis, Zrenjanin, Lapovo, Sabac and the nine municipalities of Belgrade.
Opposition leaders were sceptical that Milosevic would respond positively to the Gonzalez report.

"We do not expect him (Milosevic) to accept the findings of this (OSCE) commission. We expect further escalation, aggravation of this political crisis," said Zoran Djindjic, leader of the opposition Democratic Party.

Weeks of processions through the centre of Belgrade had come to an end on Thursday when police equipped with body armour, helmets, shields and truncheons cleared the streets and forced demonstrators back into a pedestrian square.
Prevented by police from marching through the streets again on Friday, student protesters walked in circles pretending to be prisoners.

The students blew trumpets and whistles and chanted anti-Milosevic slogans under the impassive gaze of ranks of riot police as people began arriving for the main opposition demonstration scheduled for later in the afternoon.

Observers said stated Interior Ministry concerns over the need to maintain free traffic flows in Belgrade were a clumsy but relatively effective pretence for authorities to begin reining in the anti-government protests.
Students and members of Belgrade's disaffected middle class, who have been turning out daily in their tens of thousands for the marches, are keen to avoid violence with the police.
Clashes on Tuesday, when pro- and anti-Milosevic factions fought running skirmishes in the capital before police waded in and separated the two, left at least 58 injured.
One man was critically injured when shot in the head by a government supporter. Another man died in hospital after apparently being trampled in a stampede on Tuesday.
The opposition is putting its faith in peaceful protest and international pressure on Milosevic, who needs access to lines of international credit to rescue Yugoslavia's foundering economy.

Western powers which spent much of 1996 praising Milosevic for his role in helping to broker and implement a Bosnian peace deal have now rounded on the Serbian president, lambasting his anti-democratic grip on power.
"President Milosevic has to be aware of the fact that the world is keeping its eyes on Belgrade," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Thursday.
"He should keep his hands off the demonstrators' rights and their freedom to congregate. A further escalation won't be tolerated."

The United States, Britain, France and Italy have also criticized Milosevic and the SPS. "We continue to hold Milosevic responsible for any violence which may occur," a U.S. State Department spokesman said in Washington on Thursday.

An "outer ring" of economic sanctions remains in place against Yugoslavia, the last vestige of draconian economic sanctions imposed in 1992 to punish Belgrade for its part in fomenting the Bosnian war.
Milosevic is counting on Moscow to block any U.N. Security Council attempt to reimpose sanctions which were lifted earlier this year as part of the Bosnian peace.
